Elements & Principles Lab

Learn the elements of art and principles of design by playing with works by Monet, Van Gogh, Kandinsky and Hokusai.

Balance and movement

Still or moving?

Balanced is not always better. Artists sometimes unbalance a picture on purpose. When the weight piles up on one side, the picture feels like it could tip, slide or crash, and that tension reads as movement. But imbalance is not the only way to show movement: The Starry Night is balanced, yet its swirling lines never stop moving. The scales below weigh each artwork the same way as the Balance lesson.

← Most balancedMost unbalanced →
  • Weight on one sideBig or dark shapes crowd one side and leave the other open.
  • DiagonalsSlanted lines feel like they are falling or rising. Flat lines feel calm.
  • Curves that lead awayA curve pulls your eye along and away from the center.
  • Big jumps in sizeHuge next to tiny makes the eye leap from one to the other.
  • Shapes cut off by the edgeSomething half out of the frame feels like it is moving in or out.

The artworks on this page are simplified studies drawn for teaching, after works by Claude Monet, Vincent van Gogh, Wassily Kandinsky and Katsushika Hokusai. They are not reproductions. To see the real pieces, follow the museum links under each artwork.
